Traditional Romanian Mead (Mied)

Served at: Noaptea Lupilor

Approximately 1 gallon (3.8 liters)Prep 30 minutes activeCook 3-6 months (fermentation and aging)

Mead, or Mied, is an ancient alcoholic beverage made from fermented honey, water, and yeast, often enjoyed during colder months. For Noaptea Lupilor (Night of the Wolves), a traditional Romanian holiday focused on protection against evil spirits and wolves, a warming glass of homemade mead offers a comforting and historically resonant drink to ward off the chill and celebrate the season's folklore.

Ingredients

  • 3 pounds (1.36 kg) raw honey
  • 1 gallon (3.8 liters) non-chlorinated water
  • 1 packet (5 grams) wine yeast (e.g., Lalvin EC-1118)
  • 1 teaspoon yeast nutrient (optional, but recommended)
  • 1/2 teaspoon pectic enzyme (optional, for clarity)
  • Optional spices for flavor (e.g., 2 cinnamon sticks, 5-6 whole cloves, peel of 1 orange)

Method

  1. Thoroughly sanitize all brewing equipment, including your primary fermenter (a 1-gallon carboy or food-grade bucket), airlock, stopper, stirring spoon, and bottling equipment, using a food-safe sanitizer.
  2. In a large, sanitized pot, gently heat about half of the non-chlorinated water (approximately 2 quarts or 1.9 liters) to lukewarm (not boiling) and stir in the honey until completely dissolved, creating the 'must'.
  3. Remove the pot from heat. If using optional spices, add them now to steep as the must cools.
  4. Allow the honey mixture to cool completely to room temperature (around 65-75°F or 18-24°C). This is crucial to avoid killing the yeast.
  5. While the must cools, rehydrate the yeast according to package directions, usually by sprinkling it into a small amount of warm water (around 100-105°F or 38-40°C) and letting it sit for 15-20 minutes.
  6. Once the must is cooled, pour it into your sanitized primary fermenter. Add the remaining non-chlorinated water to reach the 1-gallon mark.
  7. Stir in the yeast nutrient and pectic enzyme (if using).
  8. Add the rehydrated yeast to the fermenter. Stir gently to incorporate.
  9. Securely fit the airlock and stopper onto the fermenter. Fill the airlock with sanitized water or vodka.
  10. Place the fermenter in a cool, dark place with a stable temperature (ideally 60-75°F or 15-24°C) for primary fermentation, which typically lasts 2-4 weeks. You will see bubbling in the airlock.
  11. After primary fermentation subsides (bubbling slows significantly or stops), carefully 'rack' (siphon) the mead from the primary fermenter into a clean, sanitized secondary fermenter, leaving behind any sediment at the bottom. If you used spices, remove them now.
  12. Attach a clean airlock and stopper to the secondary fermenter and allow the mead to age and clarify for another 1-3 months.
  13. Once the mead is clear and fermentation has completely stopped, sanitize your bottles and bottling equipment. Siphon the mead into bottles, leaving about 1 inch (2.5 cm) of headspace.
  14. Cap or cork the bottles. For best flavor, age the bottled mead for at least 2-3 more months, or even longer, in a cool, dark place before enjoying.

Tips

  • Always prioritize sanitization; it is the most critical step to prevent spoilage and off-flavors.
  • Experiment with different types of honey (e.g., clover, orange blossom, buckwheat) for varied flavor profiles.
  • For a sweeter mead, you can 'stabilize' it with potassium metabisulfite and potassium sorbate after fermentation, then back-sweeten with more honey before bottling.
